findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, in plain words. This covers the 'what is it' and 'why does it matter' questions right away.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The title names a second project, firstmate, without saying what it is. On Athena's own site, a newcomer may think they have landed on the wrong page until they read the second and third paragraphs, which explain that this page is a sample study.
findings.source: <title> and h1: "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"

findings.text: The next step is easy to find, and it is concrete: what you need first, how to clone, how to install, and one command to try. A newcomer knows what to do next.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the Next steps section: "git clone https://github.com/doodla/athena.git" ... "./setup.sh" ... "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The page never explains what 'predictions' are, and it shows no example of what Athena prints or the commit it makes. So the newcomer has to imagine what the result looks like.
findings.source: Next steps: "It shows how it read the request and its predictions; press Enter to run it on your repository."

findings.text: This link sits in the header next to the newcomer's next step, but it is meant for the project owner. Nothing explains what these 'proposals' are, so it is a confusing detour for a first-time visitor.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: Most of the page is a dense state-machine reading of firstmate, with exit codes, ids like t1 and c1, and its own vocabulary. It shows that Athena can trace each statement to source lines, but a newcomer who came to learn about Athena will probably skim it or give up.
findings.source: Headings "Transitions", "Counters" and "Claims and sources" (e.g. "places-held, changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11", "exit 75")

findings.text: The same ideas (yolo, green and red, captain) are explained four or more times in almost the same words. That makes the page longer and harder to scan without adding anything new.
findings.source: yolo is defined under "Words used first", again in "What firstmate is", in card t10, and in the Glossary

findings.text: The page says plainly what it did not check, which supports its claim of accountability. A newcomer can see that the claims come from reading the code, not from running it.
findings.source: "Limits of this study": "This study read the pinned tree only ... no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read."

findings.text: This closing section points to internal repository folders and does nothing for a first-time reader.
findings.source: "About this page": "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."
